questions.stem: What is the limiting reactant in a chemical reaction?

options.text: The reactant that is present in the largest amount
The reactant that is completely used up first, limiting the amount of product formed
The reactant that is most expensive
The reactant with the highest relative formula mass

questions.explanation: The limiting reactant is the one that is completely used up first during a reaction. It limits the amount of product that can be formed because once it runs out, the reaction stops. The other reactant(s) are said to be 'in excess' because some remains unreacted after the reaction.

questions.stem: In the reaction Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂, a student uses 2.4 g of Mg and excess HCl. Which statement is correct? [Ar: Mg = 24]

options.text: HCl is the limiting reactant
Mg is the limiting reactant and determines the amount of product formed
Both reactants are limiting
Neither reactant is limiting

questions.explanation: When HCl is described as 'in excess', it means there is more than enough HCl to react with all the magnesium. Therefore, magnesium is the limiting reactant - it will be completely used up first, and the amount of Mg determines how much product is formed. Some HCl will remain unreacted.

questions.stem: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. If 1 mole of N₂ is mixed with 2 moles of H₂, which is the limiting reactant?

options.text: N₂, because there is less of it
H₂, because 3 moles are needed but only 2 are available
Neither, they will both be used up
NH₃, because it is the product

questions.explanation: The equation shows 1 mol N₂ requires 3 mol H₂. We have 1 mol N₂ but only 2 mol H₂. Since 3 mol H₂ is needed but only 2 mol is available, H₂ is the limiting reactant. It's not just about which has fewer moles - you must compare the actual ratio to the required ratio from the balanced equation.

questions.stem: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃. 5.4 g of aluminium reacts with 21.3 g of chlorine. Which is the limiting reactant? [Ar: Al = 27, Cl = 35.5]

options.text: Aluminium
Chlorine
Both are used up completely
Cannot be determined

questions.explanation: Moles of Al = 5.4/27 = 0.2 mol. Moles of Cl₂ = 21.3/71 = 0.3 mol. The ratio required is 2Al : 3Cl₂. For 0.2 mol Al, we need (3/2) x 0.2 = 0.3 mol Cl₂. We have exactly 0.3 mol Cl₂. Actually both are used up exactly. But let's recheck: if we had slightly less Cl₂ (say 0.29 mol), chlorine would be limiting. With 0.3 mol, both are used up completely.

questions.stem: When the limiting reactant is completely consumed, what happens to the reaction?

options.text: The reaction reverses direction
The excess reactant starts to decompose
The reaction stops because one reactant has run out
The reaction speeds up to use the excess reactant

questions.explanation: When the limiting reactant is completely used up, the reaction stops. No more product can be formed regardless of how much excess reactant remains. Adding more of the excess reactant will not restart the reaction. To make more product, you would need to add more of the limiting reactant.
